title: Maya, the passing pull
hookLine: the pull of the passing world, attractive and fleeting, is called maya
last: NIMRATA — FIVE GUARDS AT THE DOOR.

cards: You open your phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusty knife, and you've added a jacket to a cart. Nothing bad happened.

Everything was pretty: the knife shiny, the jacket soft, the video calming. And none of it is what you meant to do with those forty minutes. It's a familiar pull: bright, sweet, and gone the moment you look away.
The Gurus had a word for it, long before phones: maya.

teach.h: AN OLD WORD, USED MANY WAYS.
teach.b: Maya is an old Indian word, and different traditions use it differently. In some Hindu schools it can mean the world as a kind of illusion. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the stress falls somewhere else.
In the Granth's telling, the world is real; the Creator made it and lives in it.
Maya is the pull of its passing parts: money, status, comfort, attachment, anything bright that promises to last and doesn't. The problem isn't that things are fake.
It's that people lean their whole weight on things that were only ever passing through. The Granth gives maya many pictures.

Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, has a short salok near the very end of the book: as a bubble rises on water and vanishes, he says, so the world is made; Nanak says, listen, friend. The bubble is real.
It even has a rainbow on it. It just isn't a place to live. Another hymn calls maya a snake that has wrapped itself around the world.
And notice what Sikh teaching does not say: run to the forest, give up your job, leave your family. The Gurus taught a householder's path: work, family, and the Name.

teach.h: IN THE WORLD, NOT OWNED BY IT.
teach.b: The ideal is to live in the middle of the bright, busy world and not be owned by it, like a lotus that grows in water and stays dry.
That's the question maya asks on an ordinary afternoon: am I using this, or is it using me?
Pretty isn't the enemy. Forgetting that it's passing is.

how: Sikhs speak of maya as the pull of wealth, status and attachment; the Gurus taught living as householders in the world, working and raising families, while remembering the Name so as not to be ruled by that pull.

o: money and wealth, and nothing more
the belief that the world is fake
the pull of the passing world

games.q: pictures of maya — tap the pairs.
p: in the world, not owned by it
the pull of the passing world

s: in the Guru Granth Sahib, maya means the world is fake
the stress is on passing, not fake: the world is real, the pull of its passing things is maya.
the Gurus taught leaving family and work to escape maya
the Gurus taught a householder's path; the ideal is to live in the world without being owned by it.
Guru Tegh Bahadur compares the world to a bubble on water
a salok near the end of the Granth: as a bubble rises and vanishes, so the world is made.

games.q: you want to be free of maya's pull. what does Sikh teaching point you toward?
o: leave home and live alone in the forest.
live in the busy world, working and caring, without being owned by it.
decide the world is an illusion and ignore it.
games.why: the Gurus taught a householder's path. like a lotus in water, the ideal is to stay in the world and not be ruled by its passing pull.

practice: Think of one pull that got you today, a screen, a purchase, a worry about how you look, a craving, and picture it clearly, the way it shines, without scolding yourself.
Now see it as a bubble on water, catching the light, and say quietly: pretty, and passing. Then let your attention come back to the breath, which is also passing, and also here.

wordCard.voice: Maya. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the pull of the passing world: bright, attractive, and gone. Not a lie, just not a home.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: maya, the pull of the passing world; in Gurbani it's often spelled and sung with three syllables.

carryVoice: Your line: pretty, and passing. A bubble on water: real, bright, and not a place to live. Until tomorrow.
